message:
QUESTION:
By how much did the new fertiliser increase wheat yield in the on-farm trial, is it profitable at current prices, and should the farm business adopt it?

DATA:
On-farm fertiliser trial, wheat, clay-loam fields, one season. Four field blocks. In each block, one plot received the new fertiliser and an adjacent plot received standard practice (control). Yields in tonnes per hectare (t/ha):

| Block | Control | New fertiliser |
| 1 | 7.2 | 7.9 |
| 2 | 6.8 | 7.3 |
| 3 | 8.1 | 8.5 |
| 4 | 5.9 | 7.6 |

Field log: in June, the Block 4 control plot was waterlogged for about 10 days after a field drain blocked. The Block 4 fertiliser plot, on slightly higher ground, was not affected. No other plots had problems during the season.

Economics:
- The new fertiliser costs £60/ha more than standard practice.
- Grain price: £180 per tonne.
- Application and other costs are the same for both treatments.

The farm business also has sandy-soil holdings in the east of the county, which were not part of the trial. Sandy soils hold less water and nutrients than clay loam.

KNOWN FLAWS:
F1. [misreport] Block 3's gain was 0.4 t/ha (8.5 − 8.1), below half a tonne, as the draft's own next sentence shows. CORRECTION: Gains ranged from 0.4 to 1.7 t/ha; three of four blocks gained 0.5 t/ha or more.
F2. [omission] Ignores the field-log note that the Block 4 control plot was waterlogged while its paired fertiliser plot was not. This inflates the Block 4 difference (1.7 t/ha) and hence the mean; the draft even reads it as the fertiliser 'helping most where conditions are hardest'. CORRECTION: Excluding Block 4, the mean gain is (0.7 + 0.5 + 0.4) / 3 = 0.53 t/ha, worth £96/ha, for a net gain of about £36/ha rather than £88.50 (or the draft's £108.50).
F3. [calculation] 0.825 × 180 = £148.50, not £168.50. CORRECTION: £148.50/ha gross; net £88.50/ha on all four blocks (about £35,400 on 400 ha, not 'over £43,000').
F4. [inference] Generalises a one-season, four-block clay-loam result to sandy soils that were not tested and that behave differently. CORRECTION: The trial supports a (smaller) estimate for clay loam only. Sandy-soil response is unknown and needs its own trial.

EXTENSIONS:
- Paired t-test: on all four blocks, mean difference 0.825, SD about 0.60, t of about 2.8 on 3 df (p of about 0.07); excluding Block 4, mean 0.53, SD about 0.15, t of about 6.0 on 2 df (p of about 0.03). Note the tiny sample either way.
- Break-even yield gain is £60 / £180 = 0.33 t/ha. Even the conservative 0.53 t/ha clears it, but with little margin. Show how the net gain varies with grain price (e.g. at £140/t the conservative estimate nets only about £15/ha).
- Recommend a multi-season trial with more blocks and randomised plot positions within blocks, so that drainage or elevation cannot systematically favour one treatment.

FINAL VERSION:
# New Fertiliser Trial: Results and Recommendation

## Summary

- **Yield gain:** about **0.53 t/ha (about 7%)** on clay loam. This comes from the three blocks that give a fair comparison. Block 4 is excluded because its control plot was waterlogged. Including it would inflate the average to 0.825 t/ha.
- **Profitability:** at £180/t and £60/ha extra cost, the fertiliser breaks even at a gain of **0.33 t/ha**. The best estimate gives about **+£36/ha** net. There is roughly a **90% chance** the true gain is above break-even. With only three comparisons from one season, a small loss cannot be ruled out.
- **Recommendation:** do not adopt across the whole business yet.
  - On clay loam, use it on part of the area next season, set up as a larger, randomised trial.
  - Do not use it on the sandy soils until it has been trialled there.

## Design

The trial used four blocks on clay-loam fields over one season. In each block, one plot got the new fertiliser and an adjacent plot got standard practice. Comparing the two plots within a block removes most soil and drainage differences between blocks. This only works if the two plots in a block are comparable and experience the same conditions apart from the treatment. Block 4 shows what happens when they don't.

## Yields and the Block 4 problem

| Block | Control | New fertiliser | Gain (t/ha) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 7.2 | 7.9 | 0.7 |
| 2 | 6.8 | 7.3 | 0.5 |
| 3 | 8.1 | 8.5 | 0.4 |
| 4 | 5.9* | 7.6 | 1.7* |

\*In June, the Block 4 control plot was waterlogged for about 10 days after a field drain blocked. The fertiliser plot, on slightly higher ground, was not affected.

The Block 4 comparison is **confounded**:
- Its control yield of 5.9 t/ha is the lowest in the trial, very likely because of the waterlogging.
- Its fertiliser plot yield of 7.6 t/ha is in line with the other blocks. The large 1.7 t/ha gap therefore comes from a depressed control, not an unusually strong fertiliser response.
- It is not evidence that the fertiliser "helps most under stress." The fertiliser plot was never stressed.

**Block 4 is excluded from the effect estimate.** The exclusion rests on a problem recorded in the field log during the season, not on the yield result looking unusual.

## Estimated effect (Blocks 1–3)

- **Mean gain:** (0.7 + 0.5 + 0.4) / 3 = **0.53 t/ha**.
- **Relative gain:** the mean control yield in Blocks 1–3 is 7.37 t/ha, so the gain is about **7%**.
- **Consistency:** the gain was positive in all three blocks, ranging from 0.4 to 0.7 t/ha.
- **95% confidence interval: about 0.15 to 0.91 t/ha.**
  - This is a paired t-interval with 2 degrees of freedom.
  - The SD of the gains is 0.153 t/ha and the standard error is 0.088 t/ha.
  - It assumes the block differences are roughly normal, which cannot be checked with three pairs. Treat the interval as approximate.

For reference, the all-four-block mean is 0.825 t/ha (about 12%). It is biased upward and should not be used as the estimate.

## Economics

**Break-even gain** = extra cost ÷ grain price = £60 ÷ £180 = **0.33 t/ha**.

| Scenario | Gain (t/ha) | Extra revenue (£/ha) | Extra cost (£/ha) | Net (£/ha) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Break-even | 0.33 | 60 | 60 | 0 |
| **Best estimate (Blocks 1–3)** | **0.53** | **96** | **60** | **+36** |
| Lowest observed block gain | 0.40 | 72 | 60 | +12 |
| Lower 95% bound | 0.15 | 28 | 60 | −32 |
| Upper 95% bound | 0.91 | 164 | 60 | +104 |
| All four blocks (biased upward) | 0.825 | 148.50 | 60 | +88.50 |

### How likely is it to pay?

All three valid blocks cleared break-even, but Block 3 only narrowly (0.40 against 0.33). To test whether the true gain exceeds break-even:
- t = (0.533 − 0.333) / 0.088 ≈ 2.27, with 2 degrees of freedom.
- The one-sided p-value is about 0.076.
- With a standard uninformative prior, this means about a **92% probability that the true gain is above break-even**, or roughly 9 in 10.

That figure depends on the normality assumption and on a spread estimated from just three pairs. It also reflects one season only. Use it as a guide, not a precise probability.

### Risk balance per hectare

- **Expected:** about +£36/ha.
- **Plausible downside:** about −£32/ha.
- **Plausible upside:** about +£104/ha.

The odds favour a gain, and the downside per hectare is limited. That supports using it on part of the clay-loam area. It does not justify committing the whole area on one season's evidence.

### Sensitivities

- **Grain price.** At £150/t, break-even rises to 0.40 t/ha and the expected net falls to about **+£20/ha**.
- **Fertiliser price.** A rise in the £60/ha premium has the same kind of effect. Each extra £10/ha raises break-even by about 0.06 t/ha.
- **Costs that rise with yield.** The brief treats all other costs as equal. In practice, extra grain may add haulage, drying or storage costs per tonne.
  - At £10/t, the extra 0.53 t/ha costs about £5/ha.
  - The net margin falls to about +£31/ha, and break-even rises to about 0.35 t/ha.
  - On a margin this thin, these costs are worth checking against the farm's actual figures.
- **Grain quality.** The trial did not record protein or specific weight. If the crop is sold for milling, a change in quality could move the price per tonne by more than the yield effect. This could work in either direction.

### Scale

At the best estimate, the gain is about **£3,600 per 100 ha** of clay-loam wheat per year. Multiply by the farm's actual clay-loam wheat area, which the trial data do not give.

## Scope: the sandy soils

The trial covered only clay-loam fields, so **the results cannot be applied to the sandy-soil holdings in the east.** Sandy soils hold less water and fewer nutrients. That can change how a fertiliser is taken up, retained or leached. The response there could be larger, smaller, or unprofitable. Consistent results across three clay-loam blocks say nothing about a different soil type.

## Limitations

- **One season.** Weather strongly affects fertiliser response, and other years may differ.
- **Small trial.** There are three usable paired comparisons, with one plot per treatment per block. The uncertainty is wide, and the spread estimate itself is unreliable.
- **Confounded block.** Block 4 lost its valid comparison to waterlogging.
- **Plot placement possibly not random.** The Block 4 fertiliser plot sat on "slightly higher ground." That suggests plot positions may have been chosen rather than randomised. If so, the other blocks could contain smaller, unrecorded biases in either direction.
- **One soil type.** The trial covered clay loam only.
- **Outcomes not measured.** Grain quality and yield-dependent costs were not recorded.
- **Statistical assumptions.** The interval and probability figures assume roughly normal block differences.

## Recommendation

1. **Do not adopt across the whole business on this evidence.** In particular, do not extend it to the sandy-soil farms.
2. **Clay loam: limited use next season, run as a trial.**
   - The likely return is modest, about +£36/ha.
   - There is roughly a 90% chance of beating break-even, and the downside is limited.
   - Using it on part of the clay-loam area captures the probable gain while gathering the evidence for a full decision.
3. **Design next season's trial better:**
   - **Use at least eight blocks.** If the block-to-block spread is similar to this year's (SD about 0.15 t/ha), eight pairs would give a 95% CI of about ±0.13 t/ha. That is narrow enough to tell a 0.53 t/ha gain apart from the 0.33 t/ha break-even. This year's spread comes from only three pairs, so allow some margin, for example ten blocks.
   - Replicate plots within blocks where practical.
   - **Randomise** which plot in each block gets the fertiliser.
   - Make sure paired plots share the same drainage and elevation.
   - Record grain quality (protein, specific weight) as well as yield.
   - Keep the field log, as was done this year.
4. **Set the decision rule in advance.** Adopt fully on clay loam if, after the second season, the pooled estimate's lower 90% confidence bound is above break-even at that season's prices, including any per-tonne costs.
5. **Run a separate trial on the sandy soils** before any use there.
6. **Fix the Block 4 drain.** Re-run Block 4 next season only if both of its plots can be given comparable conditions.
7. **Re-assess at each season's prices.** Recompute the break-even gain before any wider rollout: (extra fertiliser cost) ÷ (grain price − per-tonne costs).
